rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Abraham pericope narrates the Quranic case for divine Oneness and Transcendence, evident to sincere observers of the universe.
rows.anchor: This pericope about Abraham and his people demonstrates in narrative form the Quranic argument for God’s Oneness and Transcendence

rows.speaker: IK, R
rows.claim: One interpretation says Abraham feigned the celestial identifications to show his idolatrous people that all changing things are temporal, unlike God.
rows.anchor: only feigned them to make the point to his idolatrous people that all things are temporal and subject to change save for the One God (IK, R)

rows.speaker: Sy, Ṭ, Ṭū
rows.claim: Another interpretation treats the episode as Abraham's genuine intellectual deduction of God's Oneness from the ephemerality of created things.
rows.anchor: a genuine process of intellectual deduction through which Abraham came to know the Oneness of God by observing the ephemerality of all created things (Sy, Ṭ, Ṭū)

rows.speaker: R, Ṭ
rows.claim: A legend says a king, sometimes identified as Nimrod, feared a prophesied boy; Abraham's mother hid him in a cave, Gabriel nurtured him, and he successively mistook a star, moon, and sun for his Lord.
rows.anchor: the king in the region—whom some identify as Nimrod (also see 2:258c)—dreamed that a boy would be born who would usurp his power

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The cave-birth legend has no Quranic or Biblical basis, combines themes from other prophetic narratives, and raises theological problems.
rows.anchor: This story, which has no basis in the Quranic or Biblical accounts of Abraham’s early life, seems to amalgamate several thematic elements

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some object that a prophet's temporary identification of created things with God would constitute idolatry.
rows.anchor: Some objected to the idea that a prophet could mistakenly identify, even temporarily, a created reality, such as a star, with God, since this is a form of shirk

rows.speaker: IK, R, Ṭū
rows.claim: A response says Abraham made the mistaken identification as a young child, before religious responsibility and prophethood.
rows.anchor: when he was still a young child, before the age of religious responsibility and before he became a prophet (IK, R, Ṭū)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Even on the deduction reading, revelation is involved: God shows Abraham the dominion and calls his argument one given to him.
rows.anchor: in v. 75 it is God who shows Abraham the dominion of the heavens and the earth

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The readings can be reconciled: Abraham may feign the argument for his people while drawing on an earlier, inspired reflection that culminated in certainty about Oneness.
rows.anchor: his demonstration may reflect an earlier process of intellectual deduction that was inspired by his wonder at the celestial bodies

rows.speaker: Sufi commentators
rows.claim: Sufi commentators read the celestial sequence as progressive spiritual illumination and increasing certainty; each body's setting marks the limits of a station and a trial before greater illumination.
rows.anchor: Sufi commentators have tended to see this passage as a symbol for progressive spiritual illumination or increasing levels of spiritual certitude

rows.speaker: al-Qushayrī
rows.claim: Al-Qushayrī maps the star to intellect and demonstrative proof, the moon to clarified knowledge, and the sun to the brilliant light of gnosis.
rows.anchor: the star represents the intellect that first witnesses the truth through demonstrative proof

rows.speaker: al-Qushayrī
rows.claim: Al-Qushayrī interprets Abraham's wonder as first seeing created things through God, then for God, and finally effacing all things in God.
rows.anchor: he interprets Abraham’s marveling at these three celestial bodies as his first seeing created things through God, then seeing them for God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Azar is named as Abraham's father only in this Quranic verse.
rows.anchor: Azar is given as the name of Abraham’s father in the Quran, although only in this verse

rows.speaker: IK, JJ, R, Ṭ
rows.claim: Some commentators identify the Biblical name Terah as a second or alternate name for Azar.
rows.anchor: Terah may have been a second or alternate name for him (IK, JJ, R, Ṭ)

rows.speaker: IK, R, Ṭ
rows.claim: Some say Azar was an idol's name and Abraham used it to disparage his father's idol worship.
rows.anchor: Azar was the name of an idol, and Abraham calls his father by this name as a way of disparaging his idol worship (IK, R, Ṭ)

rows.speaker: R, Ṭū
rows.claim: Others say Azar was Abraham's uncle, called father in the broad sense of an older paternal relative.
rows.anchor: Azar was Abraham’s uncle (R,Ṭū), who is referred to as his father in the general sense

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: The uncle interpretation was partly motivated by the Bible's spiritually neutral Terah versus the Quranic Azar, an idol worshipper and maker of idols.
rows.anchor: although Terah is a spiritually neutral figure in the Bible, Azar is identified not only as an idol worshipper, but as a maker of idols (Ṭ)

rows.speaker: Muslims, particularly Shiites
rows.claim: Some Muslims, especially Shiites, maintain that a prophet's father cannot be a disbeliever or idolater.
rows.anchor: Some Muslims, particularly Shiites, hold that the father of a prophet cannot be a disbeliever or an idolater

rows.speaker: Prophet
rows.claim: A hadith invoked for prophetic-purity doctrine says God transferred the Prophet through pure loins and wombs, unsullied by pre-Islamic idolatry.
rows.anchor: citing a ḥadīth in which the Prophet says, “God transferred me from pure loins to pure wombs

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: Reading Azar as Abraham's uncle would explain Abraham's disavowal of him without conflicting with commands to maintain good relations with disbelieving parents.
rows.anchor: it would explain why Abraham can dissociate himself from him (9:114) without contradicting the Quranic injunction to maintain good relations even with disbelieving parents

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: The most literal reading is that Azar was Abraham's father and was an idolater.
rows.anchor: the most literal reading of this and other verses is that Azar was Abraham’s father and that he was an idolater (R)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's showing Abraham the dominion may mean he witnessed the wondrous celestial and terrestrial phenomena visible to people generally.
rows.anchor: may mean simply that Abraham witnessed the wondrous phenomena of the celestial and terrestrial realms that are also visible to human beings in general

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sincere observation and sound reflection on these phenomena should lead people to infer one all-powerful God.
rows.anchor: anyone who observes and reflects upon these phenomena with sincerity and a sound mind should come to the conclusion that there is an all-powerful God who is One

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: Because God gave Abraham sound judgment, he could reason from the world around him to monotheism.
rows.anchor: Since Abraham was given sound judgment by God (21:51), he was able to apply reason to his observations of the world around him

rows.speaker: al-Rāzī
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī says divine Being and Power are objectively manifest in nature but veiled for many by error and worldly preoccupation.
rows.anchor: the manifestation of God’s Being and Power in natural phenomena is always objectively observable, but is veiled for many by human error and the preoccupation with worldly things

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī says rejecting his father's idolatry gave Abraham intellectual clarity to see divine self-manifestation with the intellect's inner eye.
rows.anchor: When Abraham rejected his father’s idolatry (v. 74), he attained a new intellectual clarity that allowed him to see this Divine Self-Manifestation with the inner eye

rows.speaker: IK, R, Ṭū, Z
rows.claim: A wider interpretation is a miraculous revelation: God opened the heavens for Abraham to see its levels up to the Throne and cleaved earth to its lowest level.
rows.anchor: God split open the heavens, allowing Abraham to see all its levels up to the Divine Throne itself, and cleaved the earth so that he could see to its lowest level (IK, R, Ṭū, Z)

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī says Abraham's vision exceeded what ordinary thoughtful monotheists can attain, being granted only to the greatest prophets, such as Muhammad.
rows.anchor: Abraham experienced this Divine Self-Manifestation to an extent that is made accessible to only the greatest prophets, such as Muhammad

rows.speaker: Prophet
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī cites the Prophet's supplication asking God to show him things as they truly are.
rows.anchor: citing the Prophet’s reported supplication, “O God, show me things as they truly (and really) are!” (R)

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: Certainty may be knowledge gained after doubt or confusion is overcome through contemplation, or may result from a vision.
rows.anchor: certainty here refers to a kind of knowledge arrived at usually after a period of doubt or confusion has been overcome through reflection and contemplation (R) or as the result of a vision

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The experience of divine self-manifestation strengthens Abraham's prior aversion to idolatry and inclination toward monotheism.
rows.anchor: Abraham’s initial aversion to idolatry and inclination toward monotheism are thus strengthened through this experience of Divine Self-Manifestation

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: Alternatively, the clause can mean God showed Abraham the dominion because he was already among those possessing certainty, rewarding prior insight.
rows.anchor: This clause might also be read to mean that God showed Abraham the dominion, “because he was among those possessing certainty” (R), that is, as a reward

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although interpreters differ between genuine deduction and rhetorical performance, the rhetorical reading best fits the surrounding context of Abraham's critique and prior revelation.
rows.anchor: The latter interpretation seems to fit best the surrounding context, since Abraham’s discourse in these verses is preceded by his explicit criticism of idolatry

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: On the rhetorical reading, Abraham's repeated 'This is my Lord' is sarcastic or joking, perhaps expressing incredulity.
rows.anchor: was not made in earnest, but rather sarcastically or in jest—perhaps with a tone of incredulity

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: Alternatively, Abraham repeats his opponents' belief to set up an argument that he will gradually disprove.
rows.anchor: as a means of setting up his opponents in an argument by beginning with a repetition of his opponents’ own view

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham's similar argument at 21:51-67 supports reading the celestial discourse as a rhetorical demonstration.
rows.anchor: see 21:51–67, where Abraham takes a similar approach

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In another argument, Abraham looks at the stars and says he is sick, perhaps signaling his true view of his people's star worship.
rows.anchor: where Abraham, while engaged in an argument with his people, glances at the stars and declares, I am sick, perhaps indicating his actual view

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: Abraham's plea for guidance indicates that only God guides and may expose his people's religious status.
rows.anchor: indicates, as in v. 71, that the only guidance is God’s guidance and it was perhaps meant to indicate to his people their own religious status (R)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After the sun sets, Abraham disavows his people's partners; similar disavowals occur from Abraham, Muhammad, and Hūd.
rows.anchor: similar statements are made by Abraham in 43:26 and 60:4 as well as by Muhammad in v. 19 and the Arabian prophet Hūd in 11:54

rows.speaker: IK, R
rows.claim: The celestial argument applies to stone idols if they represented celestial deities worshipped by Abraham's people.
rows.anchor: the idols served as representations of celestial deities worshipped by his people (IK, R)

rows.speaker: Ṭū
rows.claim: Alternatively, if even sublime moving celestial bodies are ephemeral, worshipping immobile stone idols is still more nonsensical.
rows.anchor: if even the celestial bodies, which travel through the sky and seem so sublime, can be shown to be ephemeral, it was all the more nonsensical to worship stone idols

rows.speaker: JJ, R
rows.claim: Some commentators say Abraham's people included astrologers who thought celestial bodies waxed in influence and waned in power; al-Rāzī says the argument from waning should persuade them.
rows.anchor: among Abraham’s people were astrologers (JJ, R), who considered a celestial body to be influential when it was waxing and weak and ineffectual when it was waning

rows.speaker: IK, JJ
rows.claim: Some identify the star Abraham saw as Venus.
rows.anchor: the star, which some identify as Venus (IK, JJ)

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: The star, moon, and sun were the brightest and so were considered the most powerful of the seven celestial bodies reportedly worshipped by Abraham's people.
rows.anchor: the brightest and therefore considered the most powerful of the seven celestial bodies reportedly worshipped by Abraham’s people (IK)

rows.speaker: R, Ṭū
rows.claim: The passage teaches that truth is not wholly self-evident yet cannot rest on blind imitation; certainty requires sincere reflection and clear proofs from creation.
rows.anchor: religious truth is not entirely self-evident (R, Ṭū), neither can it be based simply upon blind imitation (R)

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: Turning one's face to God means orienting one's whole being toward worship and obedience.
rows.anchor: orient one’s whole being toward the worship and obedience of God (R)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥanīf is used predominantly for Abraham in the Quran.
rows.anchor: Ḥanīf is used predominantly in connection with Abraham in the Quran

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥanīf also denotes pure monotheism avoiding every form of idolatry.
rows.anchor: elsewhere to denote a pure monotheism that avoids all manner of idolatry

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran also associates ḥanīf with Muhammad before and after his prophetic mission.
rows.anchor: it is also associated with the Prophet Muhammad both before and after the onset of his prophetic mission

rows.speaker: R, Ṭ
rows.claim: Abraham's people disputed by appealing to ancestral custom, objecting to worship of one God, or threatening harm from their idols.
rows.anchor: their false deities and idols would bring harm upon him for his rejection of them (R, Ṭ)

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: Abraham asks how vain arguments could affect someone guided by God and notes that idols can bring neither harm nor benefit.
rows.anchor: one, such as himself, who has been guided by God, and how they can hope to frighten him by invoking the partners

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: Abraham fears only what comes from God; fearing the alleged partners would only occur if God willed to test him.
rows.anchor: he fears only what comes from God, and if he were to fear the partners his people ascribe to Him, it would only be as a result of God’s Will to test him in some way (R)

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: God's encompassing Knowledge means all things occur according to His Wisdom and Knowledge.
rows.anchor: everything occurs according to His Wisdom (R) and Knowledge

rows.speaker: R, Ṭ
rows.claim: The lack of authority for the partners means there is no proof of their reality.
rows.anchor: no proof of their reality (R, Ṭ; see also 7:33, 71; 12:40; 22:71; 53:23)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The security at issue is freedom from divine punishment, and the answer is that believers who do not obscure faith through wrongdoing are secure and guided.
rows.anchor: He challenges them as to which of the two parties, he or they, has greater right to security, meaning from Divine punishment

rows.speaker: IK, Ṭ
rows.claim: The wrongdoing that obscures belief is specifically shirk, or idolatry.
rows.anchor: those who do not obscure their belief in God through shirk, or idolatry (IK, Ṭ)

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: Some understand the secure believers as those who combine faith with good works of every kind.
rows.anchor: For some, this refers to those who combine their faith with good works of all kinds (R)

rows.speaker: Prophet
rows.claim: When Companions feared that no one could avoid all wrongdoing, the Prophet clarified that wrongdoing here means idolatry.
rows.anchor: The Prophet responded by indicating that what is meantby wrongdoing here is precisely idolatry

rows.speaker: Prophet
rows.claim: The Prophet says the secure and guided are thankful in ease, patient in deprivation, seek forgiveness after wrongdoing, and forgive those who wrong them.
rows.anchor: thankful when they receive, who are patient when they are denied, who seek forgiveness when they have done wrong

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: 'Our argument' can refer to Abraham's security argument in 6:80-82, his celestial argument in 6:76-78, or both.
rows.anchor: That was Our argument refers to either the argument about who should fear God’s punishment and who should feel secure from it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran portrays Abraham repeatedly making rhetorical and dramatic arguments for monotheism and against idolatry.
rows.anchor: The Quranic account of Abraham portrays him as engaging in several rhetorical and sometimes dramatic arguments with his people regarding the truth of monotheism

rows.speaker: al-Rāzī
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī says Abraham appears in arguments against Makkan idolaters because Arabs revered him as an ancestor and Jews and Christians esteemed him too.
rows.anchor: Al-Rāzī observes that the Quran frequently invokes the story of Abraham in the context of the Prophet’s arguments with the Makkan idolaters

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran also invokes Abraham against exclusivist religious claims attributed to Jews and Christians.
rows.anchor: Abraham is also invoked in Quranic arguments against certain exclusivist religious claims attributed to Jews and Christians

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham is presented as a master of argumentation and a model for Quranic arguments against claims made by Jews, Christians, and idolaters.
rows.anchor: Abraham is both the master of argumentation and an important example for the Quran’s own arguments

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran instructs believers to argue clearly and beautifully and teaches that God has the conclusive argument.
rows.anchor: argue with their religious opponents in a manner that is clear (18:22) and beautiful (16:125)

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: 'Degrees' may mean worldly provision and power allotted by God.
rows.anchor: degrees of provision and power apportioned in this life (6:165; 43:32)

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: Another interpretation takes the degrees as ranks of divine reward for virtuous deeds.
rows.anchor: degrees of Divine reward for virtuous action (4:95–96; 9:20; 46:19)

rows.speaker: JJ
rows.claim: A further reading understands the degrees as knowledge and wisdom, since ranks elsewhere connect specifically with knowledge.
rows.anchor: degrees of knowledge and wisdom (JJ), since elsewhere the idea of degrees or ranks is connected specifically with knowledge

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The degrees may also be ranks among the prophets.
rows.anchor: degrees of prophethood, since the Quran mentions degrees or ranks among the prophets

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: In context, God raised Abraham in rank by giving him an argument against his people.
rows.anchor: In this context the implication is that God raised Abraham in degrees by virtue of the argument that He gave him against his people (R)

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī takes this verse as evidence against literalists who disparage religious argumentation, since God raises Abraham through the argument He gave him.
rows.anchor: For al-Rāzī, this verse is evidence that the literalists who disparage the use of argumentation in religion are wrong

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In response to prohibitions invented by idolaters, the Prophet is told to recite the prohibitions established by authentic revelation.
rows.anchor: In response to the false prohibitions the idolaters have invented for themselves, the Prophet is instructed to recite that which your Lord has forbidden through authentic revelation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The list here gathers prohibitions also stated elsewhere in the Quran.
rows.anchor: The list of prohibitions in these two verses brings together those mentioned elsewhere in the Quran

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ban on associating partners with God covers every form of shirk, including worship of idols, celestial bodies, and jinn mentioned in this surah.
rows.anchor: the admonition against shirk here refers to all its forms

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The paired commands to worship God alone and honor parents recur elsewhere, linking proper worship with filial reverence and care.
rows.anchor: it indicates the importance of filial piety and suggests a relationship between proper worship of God and reverence and care for parents

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: Human beings owe parents greatly because of their extensive care when the children were young, so parental duty follows worship of God.
rows.anchor: human beings are most indebted to their parents, given the extensive and solicitous care they were provided when they were young

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The warning against killing children for fear of poverty directs parents to trust God to provide for them and their children.
rows.anchor: indicating that they should rely upon God to provide for the needs of themselves and their children

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Killing a protected person is forbidden except as a warranted capital punishment, such as for murder or waging war against God and His Messenger.
rows.anchor: when it is warranted as a punishment for capital transgression, such as for murder or“waging war against God and His Messenger”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Outward and inward indecencies mean public and private forms of wrongdoing.
rows.anchor: which often connotes specifically sexual transgression (see 4:15c; 4:22c), but which here more likely refers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although fawāḥish often means sexual transgression, here it more likely means serious sins and moral transgressions generally.
rows.anchor: but which here more likely refers to serious sins and moral transgressions of all sorts

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: Avoiding sin in both public and private demonstrates true piety; private sin after public restraint shows fear of blame rather than obedience to God.
rows.anchor: if one were to avoid sin publicly, but commit it privately, it would indicate that one’s motivation was simply to avoid public blame and not to obey God (R)

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī classifies the five commands or prohibitions in 6:151 as outward sins and the four prohibitions in 6:152 as inward, private sins.
rows.anchor: v. 151 contains five commands or prohibitions that can all be said to pertain to outward sin, while v. 152 contains four prohibitions that relate to inward sin (R)

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Some define inward sin as an intention to sin formed in the heart.
rows.anchor: Some define “inward sin” as the intention to sin formulated in the heart (Q)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A well-known hadith-based principle says deeds depend on intentions, so reward or punishment for an act depends on its agent's intention.
rows.anchor: “Deeds are according to intentions,” meaning that the reward or punishment for a given act is dependent upon the intention of the one who commits it

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: A guardian must keep an orphan's property in trust until knowledge and wisdom mature; maturity is qualitative rather than a fixed age.
rows.anchor: a guardian should hold the orphan’s property in trust until the orphan reaches the age when knowledge and wisdom are sufficiently developed (R)—a standard that is qualitative

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: One view allows an impoverished guardian to take a small amount from the orphan's property, provided it is repaid when possible.
rows.anchor: when he is able, or to the guardian’s right to use the orphan’s property in a way that might help maintain or improve it (Ṭ)

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: Alternatively, the guardian may use orphan property in a way that maintains or improves its value.
rows.anchor: the guardian’s right to use the orphan’s property in a way that might help maintain or improve it (Ṭ)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Giving full measure and weight justly requires fairness and probity in commerce and business.
rows.anchor: To observe fully the measure and the balance with justice refers to the requirement to engage in commerce and business transactions with probity and fairness

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's not burdening a soul beyond its capacity is a central Islamic doctrine repeated elsewhere.
rows.anchor: is a central Islamic doctrine

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: Speaking just includes truthful testimony and integrity and truthfulness in all speech.
rows.anchor: refers to the importance of truthful testimony, but also to the requirement that one speak with integrity and truthfulness at all times (R)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran also commands honorable speech and justice in speech; this verse requires impartial justice even when the truth is against a relative.
rows.anchor: the injunction in v. 152 requires that one speak justly even if it be [against] a kinsman

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: Fulfilling God's pact here means obeying the commands and prohibitions God established.
rows.anchor: in the present verse, it is understood to mean obeying the injunctions and prohibitions established by God (Ṭ)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The straight path is the path leading to God and salvation.
rows.anchor: that leads to God and salvation (see 1:6c)

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: Most commentators identify the path specifically with Islam as taught through Muhammad's guidance and injunctions, including Quranic revelation and the Prophet's Sunnah.
rows.anchor: for most commentators it was understood to refer specifically to the religious path of Islam, defined by the guidance and injunctions brought by the Prophet Muhammad
